title: Enhancing cementitious materials with carbon black: a comprehensive review
abstract: Abstract The construction industry faces growing pressure to reduce carbon emissions, with cement production contributing approximately 7% of global CO₂ emissions. This review explores the integration of carbon black (CB), particularly pyrolyzed CB from waste tires, as a sustainable supplementary cementitious material (SCM) to improve both the environmental and mechanical performance of cementitious composites. The review discusses the physical and chemical characteristics of CB, including its particle size, surface area, porosity, and crystallographic structure, and their implications for concrete behavior. CB incorporation influences fresh properties by increasing water demand and reducing workability, although combinations with materials like fly ash can mitigate these effects. In the hardened state, CB can increase both compressive and flexural strength when used at low replacement levels (typically up to about 5% by mass of binder), but at higher CB contents these mechanical properties generally decline due to increased porosity and agglomeration effects. CB also may improve durability by refining pore structure and reducing permeability. Furthermore, it imparts multifunctional benefits such as electrical conductivity, enabling self-sensing and smart infrastructure applications. From an environmental perspective, CB reduces landfill waste and global warming potential (GWP), especially when derived from industrial by-products. Optimal replacement levels can decrease GWP by up to 35%, though excessive CB use compromises structural performance. The review also highlights knowledge gaps in dispersion techniques, microstructural interactions, and long-term durability. Future research should focus on optimizing CB dispersion, surface functionalization, and hybridization with other nanomaterials to maximize performance in smart and sustainable construction. Overall, CB emerges as a promising additive for next-generation cement-based materials, aligning with global sustainability goals and advancing multifunctional infrastructure development.
journal: Journal of Building Pathology and Rehabilitation

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The construction industry, a major contributor to global CO₂ emissions due to its energy-intensive processes and reliance on carbon-heavy materials like cement and steel, must undergo decarbonization to meet international climate targets [ 1 ]. Cement production alone is responsible for approximately 7% of global CO₂ emissions, underlining the urgent need for innovation and regulation in this sub-sector [ 2 ]. From a materials-science perspective, these pressures have driven intensive research into low-carbon binders and multifunctional cementitious composites that can reduce clinker content while maintaining or improving performance. Furthermore, comparisons of national and regional cement sector data show significant variation in emission intensity, emphasizing that locally tailored policy measures and technology adoption strategies are crucial for reducing emissions in different jurisdictions [ 3 ]. Effective carbon policies in construction, such as carbon taxes and cap-and-trade systems, can not only drive emission reductions but also raise questions of equity and competitiveness, particularly in regions with varying economic capacities [ 4 ]. In this context, energy-efficient processing routes, low-carbon admixtures, and waste-derived additives for cementitious systems become key technological levers that connect high-level policy goals with microstructural engineering at the material scale. Integrating energy-efficient technologies and carbon reduction strategies in industrial facilities, including those related to construction, has demonstrated measurable benefits in lowering emissions while maintaining productivity [ 5 ]. Additionally, managing construction and demolition waste through processes like accelerated carbonation presents a dual opportunity for CO₂ mitigation and economic gain [ 6 ]. These broader decarbonization drivers provide the motivation for exploring novel cement replacement strategies and functional additives, which is the focus of the present materials-oriented review. Comprehensive strategies targeting the construction industry’s environmental impact are thus critical for sustainable development and climate resilience [ 7 ]. In addition to these strategies, the exploration of new and innovative materials that can supplement or partially replace cement has gained significant traction in recent research. These alternative materials not only aim to reduce the environmental impact of cement production but also enhance the mechanical and durability properties of cementitious composites. Among these emerging materials, carbon black (CB) has attracted growing interest due to its potential to improve the performance of cement-based systems in various applications.

CB, especially in its pyrolyzed form from waste tires, is increasingly recognized for its potential as a sustainable supplementary cementitious material (SCM) in specific mix designs and dosage ranges, due to its fine particle size, high carbon content, and potential to partially replace cement or inert fillers while valorizing waste streams [ 8 ]. Its application in concrete has been reported to improve compressive strength and certain durability indicators when used at low to moderate replacement levels and with adequate dispersion, typically via refined pore structure and improved particle packing in the cementitious matrix; however, other studies observe neutral or even deleterious effects when CB is poorly dispersed or used at higher dosages that increase water demand and porosity [ 9 ]. The pyrolytic CB not only provides mechanical benefits but also contributes to environmental sustainability by reducing industrial waste [ 10 ]. Historically used as a rubber reinforcing filler, CB’s adaptability for use in construction materials highlights its evolving industrial value [ 11 ]. From a structural performance standpoint, when incorporated into concrete mixtures, CB can improve mechanical performance, such as tensile and flexural strength, in carefully optimized systems where dispersion and dosage are controlled. When incorporated into concrete mixtures, CB improves mechanical performance, such as tensile and flexural strength, which is crucial for structural applications [ 12 ]. It also imparts electrical conductivity to cementitious composites, enabling self-sensing and monitoring capabilities in smart infrastructure [ 13 ]. The use of CB in asphalt mixtures emphasizes its cross-disciplinary applicability in the construction industry [ 14 ]. CB-based coatings have been successfully employed for strain monitoring in concrete structures, offering cost-effective sensor alternatives [ 15 ]. It has also been used in eco-friendly cement systems to lower CO2 emissions while enhancing material performance [ 16 ].

CB has become a vital additive in cementitious materials for enhancing multifunctional properties, including electrical conductivity and self-sensing capabilities, which are critical for real-time traffic and structural monitoring [ 17 ]. The material’s effectiveness in self-sensing applications is highly dependent on moisture levels and the proper dispersion of nano carbon black [ 18 ]. While challenges like dispersion and integration costs exist, CB has been shown to help in improving mechanical strength and conductivity [ 19 ]. Optimized content and uniform dispersion enhance hydration processes, mechanical strength, and the pore structure of cement paste, contributing to improved thermal and electrical conductivity [ 20 ]. Its ability to alter resistivity in response to stress and deformation makes it ideal for smart structural applications [ 21 ]. Furthermore, partial replacement of carbon fiber with CB reduces costs while maintaining functionalities like strain sensing [ 22 ]. Sustainable solutions including reusing pyrolytic CB waste have shown to reduce environmental impact by reducing the landfills [ 23 ]. In this way, CB-modified matrices offer a route to simultaneously address mechanical performance, sensing functionality, and resource efficiency, all of which are central themes in contemporary materials design for low-carbon infrastructure. Incorporating CB with chrysotyl nanofibers has indicated to improve resistance to cracking, while its effects on air entrainment and hydration in fly ash concrete need further research [ 24 ]. The use of CB in construction supports SDG 9, 11, 12, 13, 7, and 3 by enhancing material durability, reducing emissions, promoting resource efficiency, and contributing to sustainable infrastructure and climate action [ 25 ]. In the present work, these sustainability linkages are used primarily as a motivation, while the core emphasis is placed on the underlying chemistry, microstructure, rheology, and durability of CB-cement composites. Developments in composites further highlight CB’s role in enhancing density, strength, and multifunctionality, demonstrating its value in advanced structural applications [ 26 ].

The microstructure and morphology of CB significantly influence its interaction with cementitious materials, determining its ability to enhance reactivity [ 27 ]. If the high surface area of CB is not properly utilized, it can lead to poor dispersion and weak bonding within cement matrices, compromising strength and stability [ 28 ]. Electrically conductive grades of CB offer multifunctional applications such as self-sensing, electromagnetic shielding, and conductive concrete but further research is required to optimize the dispersion of CB within the matrix to ensure uniform conductivity and improve mechanical properties [ 29 ]. Heat treatment processes modify CB’s properties, enhancing its thermal stability and conductivity, which are crucial for advanced cementitious applications, but further optimization of the heat treatment parameters is essential to fine-tune the microstructure and surface chemistry of CB for maximum performance [ 30 ]. The chemical and physical characteristics of CB influence their integration into cementitious systems, allowing tailored material performance [ 31 ]. Its role as a reinforcing filler improves tensile and compressive strength, making it essential for high-strength concrete [ 32 ]. Insights from rubber-CB composites provide valuable understanding of its mechanical contributions to cement matrices [ 33 ]. The dielectric properties of CB composites enable electromagnetic shielding and wave absorption, which are vital for high-tech construction [ 34 ]. CB’s ability to absorb electromagnetic waves enhances the functionality of cement-based materials in specialized applications [ 35 ]. When incorporated with foam cement-based composites, CB exhibits advanced electromagnetic absorption capabilities [ 36 ]. Hydration and microstructure development in CB-cement composites, especially under innovative curing techniques, play a critical role in achieving long-term performance and durability [ 37 ]. Its application in strain-monitoring smart coatings further highlights its potential for real-time structural health assessment [ 38 ]. Recycled CB, derived from scrapped materials, aligns with environmentally sustainable practices and reduces waste and its thermal properties and resistance to environmental stressors provide thermal insulation and durability, contributing to energy-efficient constructions [ 39 ]. Introduction methods for CB additives in fine-grained concretes influence their dispersion and effectiveness in enhancing material properties [ 40 ]. CB improves the setting and mechanical properties of mortar while enabling electrical functionalities for smart applications [ 41 ]. Multifunctional applications of CB include combining mechanical reinforcement with electrical conductivity, thus bridging the gap between traditional and modern construction needs [ 42 ]. Finally, its evolution as a reinforcing filler underscores its enduring relevance and adaptability in the development of innovative cementitious systems [ 43 ].CB, despite its vast potential, still presents challenges in optimizing its integration into cementitious systems, particularly regarding achieving uniform dispersion, enhancing interfacial bonding, and maintaining long-term stability. More research is necessary to explore advanced modification techniques, such as surface functionalization and hybridization with other nanomaterials, to fine-tune its properties for enhanced performance in multifunctional cementitious applications. This review paper is conducted to provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of CB in cement-based materials, highlight recent advancements, and identify critical gaps in the current knowledge to guide future research direction.

sections.heading: Sources of carbon black
paragraphs: CB is predominantly derived as a by-product of industrial processes and waste materials involving processes such as thermal decomposition, incomplete combustion, and pyrolysis of hydrocarbons. The furnace black process involves the partial combustion and pyrolysis of aromatic hydrocarbons at high temperatures to produce CB, with byproducts like tail gas that can be recovered for energy [ 44 ]. Researchers explore the thermal decomposition of natural gas, emphasizing the roles of reactor temperature and feedstock flow rates in maximizing CB yield [ 45 ]. The pyrolysis process provides a promising pathway to convert waste tires into valuable byproducts, including CB, which holds significant industrial potential. The potential for high-value utilization of waste tires by modifying CB properties was discussed, highlighting its critical role in promoting sustainable waste management practices [ 46 ]. Similarly, optimization techniques were stated to improve the properties of pyrolytic residues, enabling their application as commercial-grade CB [ 47 ]. A sustainable method emphasizing high yield and scalability was reported for producing CB nanoparticles from waste tires through a one-step thermal decomposition process [ 48 ]. One of the earlier works laid the groundwork for efficient tire pyrolysis processes, emphasizing the importance of process parameters in enhancing CB yield and quality [ 49 ] (Fig.  1 ).
Fig. 1 Production Pathways of CB from Various Feedstocks: Pyrolysis, Combustion, and Thermal Cracking Technique

High-temperature pyrolysis was investigated to produce high-quality CB, elucidating the chemical and physical mechanisms that determine product consistency and purity [ 50 ]. A comprehensive analysis of physicochemical treatments required to recover CB from waste automobile tires was explored, establishing the basis for modern recycling practices [ 51 ]. Building on this, chemical modifications to further enhance the structural and functional properties of recycled CB were examined, positioning it as a viable substitute for virgin materials [ 52 ]. Oil Furnace Process delves into parametric studies of CB oil furnaces, shedding light on optimizing yield and quality through temperature and feedstock control [ 53 ]. Agricultural bio-wastes, such as coconut shells, rice husks, and sawdust, serve as sustainable precursors to produce CB due to their abundance and lignocellulosic composition. These bio-wastes can be converted into activated carbon through physical and chemical activation techniques using agents like steam, CO₂, KOH, and H₃PO₄, with optimization of parameters such as temperature, activation time, and impregnation ratios being crucial for maximizing carbon yield and surface properties [ 54 ]. The pyrolysis of agricultural residues involves the decomposition of biomass at high temperatures in an inert atmosphere, with parameters such as heating rate, particle size, and residence time significantly influencing the efficiency and quality of the CB produced [ 55 ]. The utilization of waste CB highlights its dual role in reducing waste and providing valuable material for construction, contributing to circular economy initiatives [ 56 ].

sections.heading: Particle size and distribution
paragraphs: The particle size of CB is a key factor influencing its functionality across various applications, particularly in cementitious materials [ 57 ,  58 ]. Depending on the grade and production process, particle size directly affects the optical, electrical, and mechanical properties of the material [ 15 ]. A narrow and controlled particle size distribution is preferred, as it ensures uniform dispersion within the matrix [ 59 ]. The particle size distribution of commercially available carbon black grades reveals systematic relationships between particle dimensions and their suitability for cement and concrete applications.

The standard method for determining particle size distribution is transmission electron microscopy (TEM), as outlined in ASTM D3849–22 [ 60 ]. While TEM provides valuable insights, it has limitations in determining the mean particle size (MPS). Instead, the Statistical Thickness Surface Area (STSA) method is often used for MPS determination due to its accuracy in correlating surface area with particle dimensions. Additionally, precise particle boundaries cannot be defined using TEM, leading researchers to explore alternative techniques such as dynamic light scattering (DLS) [ 61 ], also known as intensity fluctuation spectroscopy and the differential mobility technique. 2 illustrates the particle size distribution for different CB grades, showing that a higher percentage of particles tend to have smaller diameters.

Beyond individual particle size, the overall distribution within a sample significantly impacts consistency in performance when CB is incorporated into formulations. A well-regulated particle size distribution minimizes agglomeration, facilitating better interaction with other components. Production method variations also introduce differences in particle size distribution, which, in turn, affect the properties of the final product [ 62 ,  63 ] (Fig.  2 ).
Fig. 2 Particle size distribution of some commercially available CB grades [ 62 ]

The particle size of CB may significantly affect the properties of cementitious materials by altering hydration dynamics, microstructure development, and mechanical performance. Smaller CB particles, with their high surface area, may act as nucleation sites that accelerate hydration, potentially enhancing the formation of calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gel, which contributes to increased strength and durability of the matrix. Additionally, finely dispersed CB particles can improve the packing density of the cementitious system, reducing porosity and potentially leading to higher compressive strength and lower permeability. On the other hand, larger particle sizes may cause agglomeration, which could disrupt the homogeneity of the mixture and introduce weak points within the matrix. The careful control of CB particle size may also improve the thermal and electrical conductivity of cementitious materials, making them suitable for applications where self-sensing or electromagnetic shielding properties are desired.

sections.heading: Density and specific gravity
paragraphs: The density of CB is a key property that affects its behaviour in composite materials. It is primarily governed by the production process and the extent of particle aggregation. CB typically exhibits a high specific gravity, generally ranging between 1.8 and 2.1 [ 64 ]. The specific gravity plays a crucial role in determining its dispersion, reinforcement potential, and interaction with other components in a mixture, such as cement in concrete or polymers in composite material [ 65 ].

Several methods have been developed over the years to determine the density of CBs. The most precise measurements are obtained using X-ray diffraction (XRD), which determines density based on atomic spacing [ 47 ]. The density measured via XRD is referred to as the true material density, as it provides a value independent of external factors like porosity. However, in practical applications, pycnometer measurements are more commonly employed to determine density and is influenced by the porosity of the CB and the ability of the immersion fluid to wet the solid surface [ 66 ]. A summary of true and apparent densities for various CB types, along with their respective production methods, is provided in Table  1 .

sections.heading: Crystallographic structure
paragraphs: Fig. 3 Structure of carbon black [ 72 ]
Fig. 4 Structure of Functionalized CB with Oxygenated Groups [ 77 ,  78 ].

The Fig.  4  illustrates a commonly accepted structural model for the crystallographic framework of carbon black, in which small, graphene-like aromatic layers are decorated by various oxygen-containing functional groups. The hexagonal rings represent condensed sp 2 -bonded carbon domains, analogous to nanocrystalline graphite basal planes, while defects and edge sites host functional groups such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, ketone, lactone, quinone, and pyrone moieties [ 79 ]. These surface functionalities locally distort the ideal graphitic stacking, interrupt π-electron conjugation, and create a heterogeneous structure composed of more ordered graphitic cores surrounded by disordered, oxidized edge regions [ 80 ]. In the context of cementitious systems, this mixed crystalline–amorphous character and the distribution of oxygenated sites control the surface energy, charge, and reactivity of CB particles, thereby influencing their dispersion, interaction with ions and hydrates, and ultimately their macroscopic performance [ 81 ].

sections.heading: Morphology and microstructure
paragraphs: CB’s morphology and microstructure play a crucial role in determining its performance across various applications [ 82 ,  83 ]. Fundamentally, CB is composed of nearly spherical primary particles, with diameters ranging from 10 to 100 nm, formed through the three-dimensional grouping of several discontinuous hexagonal layers (described in Sect.  Crystallographic structure ) [ 84 ,  85 ]. However, these primary particles rarely exist individually, instead, they tend to coalesce into complex, branched structures known as aggregates [ 86 ]. These aggregates represent the smallest dispersible units of CB and typically range in size from 50 to 500 nm [ 87 ]. The size and shape of aggregates differ across a long-range, influencing properties like dispersibility, viscosity, and electrical conductivity, but they are also significantly influenced by processing and mechanical handling [ 88 ]. In cementitious systems, this aggregate hierarchy controls how CB clusters fragment under shear, how many nucleation sites are exposed per unit volume, and how effectively these sites participate in C-S-H nucleation and early-age hydration kinetics. Recent work on multistep C-S-H nucleation highlights the importance of heterogeneous nano-surfaces in determining nucleus density, growth rate, and pore filling, suggesting that highly dispersed, high-surface-area CB can act as an efficient heterogeneous substrate for C-S-H cluster attachment and growth, thereby modifying both the acceleration peak and subsequent microstructural refinement in hydrated cement paste [ 89 ]. A variety of techniques can be used to determine the aggregate size of CBs, such as Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS), and Disc Centrifuge Photosedimentometry (DCP). Among the available methods, DCP is frequently used due to its cost-effectiveness and simplicity. It relies on the principle of centrifugal sedimentation and employs Stokes’ law to estimate aggregate size [ 90 ]. Beyond simple sizing, combining DCP or DLS with TEM-based image analysis enables estimation of aggregate fractal dimension, which can be linked to effective hydrodynamic radius and thus to yield stress and plastic viscosity of CB-modified cement suspensions [ 91 ]. Literature indicates that CB–C–S–H bonding is dominated by physical rather than strongly chemical mechanisms [ 92 ]. CB particles act as nano-cores around which C–S–H nucleates and densifies, refining the ITZ and improving local stiffness and compressive strength [ 93 ]. SEM and nanoscale ITZ studies show C–S–H gels wrapping CB aggregates with good mechanical interlocking but without fiber-like crack-bridging, which explains limited improvement in flexural toughness [ 94 ]. Where CB surfaces carry oxygen-containing groups, Ca-mediated interactions and hydrogen bonding with C–S–H can further stabilize the interface, but these are secondary to packing and nucleation effects [ 95 ]. The aggregate shape is also a crucial factor as it influences the absorption capacity of CBs. More branched aggregates tend to absorb higher amounts of liquids compared to aggregates with more closed structures [ 96 ]. In addition to TEM, the n-dibutyl phthalate (DBP) Absorption test (DBPA) is commonly used to provide a rough estimate of the shape of aggregates present. It relies on the absorbed volume of DBP to provide an estimate of the aggregate shapes that may be present in the CBs [ 97 ]. The aggregate shapes are categorized into four types based on detailed TEM studies, namely, (a) spherical, (b) ellipsoidal, (c) linear, and (d) branched, as illustrated in Fig.  5 . Thermal blacks have been observed to majorly consist of spherical aggregates along with low absorption capacities. The aggregate shapes composing most different CB grades are described in Table  2 . In cementitious matrices, high-DBP, highly branched structures tend to form space-spanning flocculated networks that increase static yield stress, whereas more compact, low-DBP aggregates contribute less to network formation but may act as finer packing fillers that primarily affect plastic viscosity and water demand [ 91 ]. Due to the complex and irregular nature of CB aggregates, fractal models are often applied to describe their morphology and microstructure [ 98 ,  99 ]. The fractal dimension, commonly expressed as the perimeter fractal ( Dₚ ) or the mass fractal ( Dₘ ), provides a quantitative measure of the shape and size of the aggregates. These models help in understanding the self-similar nature of aggregate structures and offer a means to correlate the microstructural features of CB with its macroscopic properties. When CB is dispersed in alkaline cement pore solution, aggregates with higher mass fractal dimension typically generate stronger, more elastic percolated networks at a given volume fraction, which in turn elevate both dynamic and static yield stresses of the paste and enhance rebuilding under rest behaviors that have been widely reported for aqueous CB gels and are consistent with rheological observations in nano-modified cement systems [ 100 ].
Fig. 5 Different Aggregate Shapes of CB and Their Morphological Variations [ 91 ].

sections.heading: BET surface area analysis
paragraphs: The surface area of CB has been determined using various methods in prior studies, with most techniques relying on the adsorption of specific molecules onto the surface [ 101 ]. Since surface area measurements are highly dependent on the choice of adsorbate, the porosity of the CB sample, and the particular grade of CB under study, the results can vary across different methodologies. Among these, the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface analysis method, developed in 1938, is the most widely used technique due to its reliability in quantifying surface area [ 102 ]. In the context of cement chemistry, the BET surface area of CB directly governs the available interface for adsorption of calcium, aluminate species, and superplasticizer polymers, thereby influencing surface charge development (zeta potential), dispersion stability, and the spatial distribution of C-S-H nuclei in the early hydration period [ 103 ]. In the BET method, nitrogen gas is commonly used as the adsorbate and is adsorbed by the CBs at cryogenic temperatures, typically achieved by immersing the CB sample in liquid nitrogen. The volume of nitrogen adsorbed in a monolayer is then measured using either single-point or multi-point continuous flow instruments [ 104 ]. While the single-point method is faster and more cost-effective, it is generally less accurate than the multi-point method, which provides a more precise estimation of surface area [ 47 ,  105 ]. Researchers have also explored the use of other inert gases such as argon, krypton, and xenon instead of nitrogen to investigate variations in adsorption behavior and improve accuracy [ 106 ]. For use in cement systems, multi-point N₂ BET or Kr BET measurements are especially valuable because they capture contributions from both external and accessible internal surfaces, which are the loci of ionic double-layer formation and superplasticizer anchoring that control dispersion, steric hindrance, and ultimately the rheology and hydration kinetics of the paste [ 107 ]. The surface areas of different CB grades measured using nitrogen BET surface analysis by Voet et al. in [ 108 ] are presented in Table  3 . The presented data also highlights the influence of production processes on the surface areas of CBs. The relatively high surface area of CB makes it effective in applications involving interaction with polymer matrices, cementitious materials, or other composite systems, thereby influencing the overall material performance [ 109 ]. In cementitious matrices, higher BET surface area generally correlates with stronger adsorption of polycarboxylate-ether superplasticizers and higher demand for dispersant to reach a given slump or yield stress, consistent with observations that more positively charged or high-surface early hydration products adsorb greater amounts of superplasticizer and strongly modify paste rheology [ 110 ].

sections.heading: Porosity and adsorption characteristics
paragraphs: The porosity of CB is a critical parameter that not only influences its properties but also affects the measurement of several key material properties, such as surface area. Porosity is determined using both gas adsorption and density techniques [ 111 ]. There are two types of porosity present in CB: open porosity and closed porosity. The information about the percentage of open and closed porosity is determined by measuring the density of CB in different media, whereas gas adsorption techniques provide information about the pore sizes [ 112 ]. In highly alkaline pore solutions, this porosity controls accessible internal surface for ion exchange and water uptake, which can delay or redistribute local saturation states and thus subtly shift the balance between dissolution, nucleation, and growth of C-S-H and ettringite in the vicinity of CB particles [ 113 ]. Open porosity in CB is predominantly made up of micropores (size < 2 nm) and can account for anywhere from 1% to 38% of the total porosity, depending on the production process [ 114 ]. Typically, the pore characteristics are determined by adsorbing a monolayer of nitrogen at various relative pressures, as outlined in  Sect. 3.3.1 . However, when dealing with exceptionally small pores (less than 0.7 nm), many researchers adopted the t-method developed by Lippens, Linsen, and DeBoer in 1964 [ 115 ]. This method involves plotting the statistical thickness of the adsorbed nitrogen against the volume of gas adsorbed. The surface areas of different commercially available CB grades are described in Table  3 . From a cement perspective, CB grades with higher microporosity can sequester mixing water and admixtures within nanometric pores, effectively increasing the apparent superplasticizer and water demand at constant w/c, whereas less porous grades act more like inert fillers with lower impact on chemical shrinkage and capillary network formation [ 107 ].

The carbon black versus BET surface area plot demonstrates a fundamental inverse power-law relationship that is critical for optimizing carbon black selection in cement and concrete applications [ 117 ]. This trend is consistent with the general inverse scaling of specific surface with primary particle size reported for furnace blacks, where surface areas decrease from roughly 140 m²/g for 15–20 nm grades to below 40 m²/g for particles larger than about 70 nm [ 89 ]. Ultra-fine carbon black grades (N110, N115) with particle sizes of 15–16 nm exhibit the highest specific surface areas, providing maximum interface availability for cement hydration acceleration and nucleation site formation, which directly translates to enhanced early-age strength development and refined microstructure in cementitious systems [ 118 ]. Such nucleation effects mirror those observed for other high-surface nano-additions, where increased densities of C-S-H nuclei lead to accelerated heat evolution and denser C-S-H networks at early ages [ 91 ]. Fine reinforcement grades (N121, N134, N220, N234) occupy the intermediate range with particles of 20–22 nm and surface areas of 116–143 m²/g, offering an optimal balance between reinforcing efficiency and workability maintenance, making them particularly suitable for high-performance concrete applications where both mechanical enhancement and processability are required [ 119 ]. The medium processing grades (N326, N330, N375, N550) demonstrate a transition zone where particle sizes increase from 28 to 50 nm while surface areas decrease proportionally to 42–93 m²/g, enabling applications in lightweight concrete systems where reduced viscosity and improved flow characteristics are prioritized over maximum reinforcement [ 120 ].

Carbon black should be distinguished from classical pozzolanic SCMs because it is largely carbonaceous and generally does not consume portlandite to form additional C–S–H, so its primary action in cement is physical rather than pozzolanic [ 121 ]. In its traditional role as a reinforcing filler, CB improves mechanical performance mainly by nano-filling and microstructure densification, where high-surface aggregates refine the pore structure and strengthen the matrix or interfacial zones without significant chemical reaction [ 122 ]. When used as a conductive additive, CB is dosed above the electrical percolation threshold so that interconnected particle networks and tunneling contacts dominate charge transport, enabling piezoresistive self-sensing behavior but only modestly influencing bulk strength [ 40 ]. At lower dosages, CB can also function as a nucleation agent, providing additional heterogeneous surfaces for early C–S–H formation in analogy with other nano-seeds, which accelerates early hydration and modestly increases early-age strength without altering clinker chemistry [ 123 ]. Finally, when CB is treated as a low-carbon SCM substitute, it primarily replaces a portion of cement clinker mass and reduces embodied CO₂ through dilution and circular use of waste-derived recovered CB, but its contribution to strength and durability arises from filler and nucleation effects rather than from true pozzolanic reactivity as defined for fly ash or slag [ 112 ]. From a rheological standpoint, the introduction of nano- to submicron carbonaceous particles typically increases both dynamic and static yield stress and enhances thixotropy at low to moderate dosages, similar to trends reported for nano-carbon suspensions and nano-reinforced cement pastes [ 124 ]. Therefore, any reported improvement in flow at higher CB contents must be interpreted carefully as it is more plausibly attributed to changes in particle packing, shifts in aggregate morphology toward less ramified structures, or increased superplasticizer dosage, rather than an intrinsic lubricating effect of CB itself [ 124 ]. Quantitatively, studies on carbon-based nanoadditions in cement pastes show that the static yield stress can increase by tens of percent at volume fractions below 1%, with accompanying increases in thixotropic rebuilding rates, unless compensated by higher superplasticizer dosages [ 125 ]. Coarse application grades (N660, N774, N990) with particles ranging from 70 to 300 nm and correspondingly low surface areas serve specialized functions in cement research, including thermal insulation applications and systems requiring minimal interference with cement hydration kinetics while maintaining electrical conductivity for self-sensing concrete development [ 126 ]. This logarithmic relationship enables cement researchers to systematically select carbon black grades based on the inverse correlation between particle fineness and surface reactivity, where smaller particles provide superior mechanical reinforcement through enhanced particle packing and C-S-H gel nucleation, while larger particles facilitate processing advantages and specialized functional properties in advanced cementitious composites [ 127 ]. However, because dispersion quality, surface chemistry, and admixture interactions strongly modulate zeta potential and adsorption, the strong correlation coefficient observed between particle size and BET surface area should be viewed as a first-order predictor of behavior rather than a stand‑alone design parameter [ 128 ]. The distribution is represented in Fig.  6 .

The unique physical and structural characteristics of CB, including its fine particle size, high surface area, and porosity, directly influence its behaviour when incorporated into cementitious systems. Thus, understanding how these properties translate into changes in workability, strength, and durability of concrete is crucial for optimising its concentration in mix design. In particular, the coupling between carbon black surface area and porosity, zeta potential, and superplasticizer adsorption governs dispersion and yield stress, while the density of heterogeneously nucleated C–S–H on carbon black surfaces influences early hydration kinetics and microstructural refinement, and the percolation of carbon black aggregates controls both mechanical reinforcement and electrical self-sensing functionality in hardened composites [ 129 ].

sections.heading: Behavior of concrete with carbon black
Workability and consistency
paragraphs: The incorporation of carbon black (CB) in concrete significantly alters the workability and consistency characteristics of the fresh mixture due to its hydrophobic nature and high specific surface area interactions with the cementitious matrix [ 130 ]. Nano-carbon black exhibits inherent hydrophobic properties and porous microstructure that fundamentally impacts the rheology of cement pastes during initial mixing, creating challenges in achieving optimal flow characteristics [ 131 ]. Studies have demonstrated that carbon black additions result in increased viscosity and reduced fluidity of fresh concrete mixtures, with the hydrophobic nature of CB particles limiting the effective water content available for cement hydration and particle lubrication [ 40 ]. The rheological behavior of carbon black-modified cement pastes demonstrates complex characteristics where the addition of CB affects both yield stress and plastic viscosity parameters, requiring careful consideration of dispersion techniques to maintain adequate workability [ 132 ]. Research indicates that carbon black nanoparticles can reduce the viscosity of cement slurry under specific conditions, which may improve pumpability and displacement efficiency in certain applications [ 133 ]. The flow properties of concrete incorporating carbon black are significantly influenced by the dispersion quality and particle interaction mechanisms, with proper dispersion being critical for maintaining acceptable consistency while achieving enhanced electrical conductivity properties [ 134 ]. The initial viscosity values of mixtures with carbon black increase due to accelerated structure formation processes resulting from enhanced particle interactions, necessitating the use of appropriate superplasticizers or chemical dispersants to optimize fresh concrete properties [ 127 ].

As discussed in previous sections, CBs are very fine particles with high surface areas, and this characteristic significantly influences the workability of concrete mixes. Several studies have investigated the incorporation of various forms of CB, such as pyrolyzed, waste-derived, and acetylene CBs, into concrete [ 9 ,  122 ]. A common observation is that adding CBs or replacing fine aggregates with CBs tends to reduce workability, as indicated by lower slump test values [ 135 ,  136 ]. In some cases, this reduction in workability has been reported to be as high as 25% for concrete mixes with up to 50% CB replacement [ 137 ]. This decline is primarily attributed to the increased water demand associated with the high surface area of CBs [ 37 ].

Interestingly, a few studies have noted that beyond a certain threshold level of CB addition or replacement, the workability of concrete may improve in some cases [ 122 ]. This phenomenon is thought to result from the aggregation behaviour of CBs, where the formation of closed aggregates could reduce or increase the overall water demand [ 137 ]. However, if branched or opened aggregates form, the workability reduces, and the consistency increases rapidly with increased CB content. These conflicting observations highlight the complex interplay between CB characteristics and concrete, suggesting that both the dosage and the aggregation of CB are critical factors in determining the workability and consistency of the mix.

In one of our research projects, we evaluated the influence of carbon black (CB) on mortar workability in systems containing Type IL cement with and without supplementary cementitious materials—specifically, fly ash and calcined clay. Carbon black plays a significant role in modifying the workability and sustainability of cement-based mixtures. When added to Portland Limestone Cement (Type IL) mortars, carbon black’s ultra-fine particles increase the paste’s viscosity by absorbing water and forming agglomerates, which in turn significantly reduce the flow of the mix. This reduction in flow as mentioned in Fig.  7  becomes more pronounced with higher carbon black contents, making the mix stiffer and harder to work with. In the context of sustainability, carbon black serves as a potential partial replacement for cement, reducing the overall carbon footprint. However, its use must be carefully balanced, as it can hinder the fresh mix’s flow unless properly adjusted with admixtures like superplasticizers or by combining it with other supplementary materials such as fly ash.
Fig. 7 Flow behavior of mortar mixes with carbon black and supplementary materials

The inclusion of fly ash or calcined clay with carbon black in these mixtures has been shown to mitigate some of the adverse effects on workability. Fly ash, with its spherical and smooth particles, helps improve flow by reducing internal friction, thereby partially compensating for the stiffening effect of carbon black. On the other hand, calcined clay, due to its high surface area and water demand, exacerbates the reduction in flow when combined with carbon black, leading to very stiff mixtures. Therefore, to optimize the benefits of carbon black while maintaining adequate workability, a well-designed mix incorporating other supplementary materials (like fly ash) and proper admixture use is crucial. This balance enables the production of sustainable, high-performance cement mixtures without sacrificing workability, ultimately contributing to both environmental and material efficiency goals.

sections.heading: Setting time and rheology
paragraphs: The incorporation of carbon black in concrete significantly influences both setting time characteristics and rheological behavior of fresh cementitious systems, with the extent of effects being dependent on the carbon black concentration and dispersion quality. The rheological properties of carbon black-modified cement pastes demonstrate complex thixotropic behavior, where the material exhibits time-dependent recovery of structure after shear deformation, significantly affecting the consistency and workability over time [ 49 ]. Carbon black incorporation leads to substantial increases in both static and dynamic yield stresses as well as equivalent plastic viscosity of cement pastes, with the relative viscosity of mixtures with carbon black being notably higher compared to non-additive cement due to enhanced particle interactions and network formation [ 138 ]. The alternating current curing of carbon black-cement conductive composites reveals that short-time electrical treatment can greatly shorten setting times by increasing hydration temperature and improving electrical resistivity, demonstrating the dual influence of carbon black on both thermal and electrical properties during the setting process [ 61 ]. Studies on cement-based sensors with carbon black subjected to various temperature and moisture conditions show that initial and final setting times remain within acceptable standards while maintaining enhanced self-sensing capabilities [ 75 ]. The thixotropic behavior of carbon black-modified cement systems is attributed to the formation of percolation networks and enhanced interparticle interactions, which create reversible structural changes under applied shear stress with corresponding recovery periods that influence the overall rheological response [ 134 ]. Temperature effects on carbon black-cement systems demonstrate accelerated structure formation processes, where increased temperatures enhance both the setting kinetics and the development of rheological properties, necessitating careful control of mixing and placement procedures [ 139 ].

The setting time of cement paste is a critical parameter that governs workability and construction scheduling. Depending on its concentration, CB can either accelerate or retard the hydration process. Several studies have explored the impact of replacing a portion of cement content with CB. A study found that replacing up to 5% of cement with CB resulted in a reduction of approximately 47% in the initial setting time and about 38% in the final setting time [ 37 ]. However, on further replacement of cement with CB, both the initial and final setting times decrease.

A slight replacement of cement with CB tends to allow it to occupy the pores within the cement matrix, thereby reducing the void ratio. This reduction in the void ratio effectively decreases the surface area of cement available for interaction with water, which delays the setting of the paste. On the other hand, when CB is added beyond a certain threshold, the material tends to aggregate (as discussed in Sect.  4.1.1), resulting in increased water absorption by the aggregates. This higher water absorption by CBs accelerates the hydration process, reducing the setting time. These observations align with the results noted in workability and consistency tests, particularly in cases where open CB aggregates are predominant. However, increased water absorption by CBs may lead to lower water availability for cement. Thus, it is also important to assess the hardened properties of concrete to understand better the implications of using CBs in concrete.

sections.heading: Compressive and flexural strength
paragraphs: Carbon black shows a clear negative effect on early flexural strength but proper carbon black concentrations can increase compressive strength, with studies reporting that carbon black addition enhances compressive strength [ 61 ]. However, these outcomes are strongly mix‑design dependent, as they are influenced by baseline water‑to‑binder ratio, cement and supplementary cementitious material contents, curing regime, and whether the carbon black surface is oxidized or otherwise functionalized; therefore, reported percentage gains should be interpreted as trend indicators rather than directly transferable design values [ 140 ]. Nano-carbon black additions in ultra-high performance concrete demonstrate the potential for mechanical property enhancement at optimized dosages [ 31 ]. These optimal conditions are typically obtained only within a narrow window of carbon black volume fraction and dispersant dosage, beyond which increased flocculation and air entrainment negate any pore-filling or nucleation benefits [ 9 ]. The compressive strength enhancement mechanisms are attributed to carbon black’s ability to fill tiny voids within cement matrices and act as nucleation sites for C-S-H gel formation, though excessive carbon black content can lead to strength deterioration due to dispersion challenges and increased porosity [ 141 ]. In addition, the strong adsorption of superplasticizers and changes in zeta potential at the carbon black–cement interface can modify packing density and internal curing conditions, which further contributes to strength evolution and helps explain discrepancies between different studies. Studies on different kinds of carbon black nanoparticles reveal that carbon black aggregates with lower structures provide the best results for both sensing ability and compressive strength, with optimal mechanical strength achieved at specific dispersant dosages [ 142 ]. The flexural strength of carbon black-modified concrete exhibits more sensitivity to carbon black additions compared to compressive strength, with research showing that nano-silica and nano-carbon black simultaneous incorporation results in decreased flexural strength with increasing carbon black content [ 143 ]. Unlike fiber‑reinforced systems, carbon black does not provide significant crack‑bridging across macro‑cracks, and CB‑modified concretes often show increased brittleness or reduced post‑peak toughness even when compressive strength is improved, underscoring that enhancements in compressive behavior do not necessarily translate into better flexural or fracture performance [ 144 ]. Pyrolyzed carbon black derived from waste tires demonstrates significant potential for strength enhancement [145].

The incorporation of CB into concrete significantly impacts its hardened properties. Much like its effects on fresh properties, the influence on compressive and flexural strength highly depends on the concentration and type of CB used. For clarity, most published results refer to partial replacement of cement or fine aggregate by mass, generally within the range of about 0.5–10% by binder mass, under standard curing in water or moist conditions at 20–25 °C, and outside these ranges, mechanical responses can deviate significantly [ 29 ]. A few studies have been conducted to evaluate the compressive and flexural strength of concrete containing pyrolyzed CBs (PCBs) and waste CBs (CBs). Studies on the effect of PCBs and CBs, respectively, revealed that an increase in CB content up to about 5% leads to an improvement in compressive strength (up to a 32% increase with PCBs and a 25% increase with CBs). These reported gains were obtained for specific reference mixes and therefore should be seen as demonstrating the existence of an optimum rather than as universal target values. It was also observed that the 7-day and 28-day compressive strength varied with similar ratios, indicating a consistent effect on early- and late-age strength [ 37 ,  137 ]. This suggests that, within the optimal dosage range, carbon black primarily modifies microstructural densification rather than fundamentally altering the relative rate of strength gain over time. However, further increases in CB content reversed the improvements. Beyond approximately 5%, the compressive strength declined, eventually returning to values near those of the control mix at around 10% CB replacement, and further additions led to further degradation of the strength. A similar trend is observed for flexural strength, although the improvements in strength were not as pronounced. One of the studies showed that flexural strength increases by about 5% with CB addition up to 10%, after which further increases in CB content result in reduced flexural strength [ 37 ]. In many cases, even when modest increases in flexural strength are reported at low dosages, load–deflection curves and fracture tests reveal a more brittle response with steeper post‑peak softening, highlighting that carbon black alone cannot replicate the toughness and crack‑bridging efficiency provided by micro‑ or macro‑fibers [ 126 ].

The variation in strength can be attributed to multiple factors. A small increase in the CB content fills up the micro voids in concrete, as described in Sect. 4.1.2, leading to increased strength, even though the cement content decreases. However, after a certain threshold this filling effect cannot balance the decrease in cement content, thus reducing the strength for any further increase in CB content. Additionally, as described in Sect. 4.1.2, a reduction in water available for hydration due to the formation of open aggregates of CB may also lead to incomplete hydration, thus decreasing strength. Dispersion efficiency, mixing energy, and the compatibility between carbon black and chemical admixtures therefore become key parameters, as insufficient dispersion accelerates the transition from beneficial void filling and nucleation to detrimental agglomeration, entrapped air, and weak interfacial zones [ 134 ]. Mechanically, the observed strength trends with increasing CB content can be rationalized by three coupled mechanisms [145]. At low dosages, nano‑filling and heterogeneous nucleation of C–S–H on CB surfaces refine the pore structure and strengthen the ITZ, leading to modest compressive strength gains [ 145 ]. At intermediate and high dosages, however, strong van der Waals attraction between CB aggregates and competitive adsorption of superplasticizers promote flocculation, entrapped air, and locally higher effective w/b, which undermine both compressive and flexural strength despite the nominal cement replacement level [ 146 ]. Finally, because CB particles do not bridge macro‑cracks, conductivity gains originate from the formation of percolated CB networks and tunneling contacts rather than from any fiber‑like crack‑bridging, so enhancements in self‑sensing capability are inherently decoupled from and can even oppose improvements in flexural toughness [ 147 ]. A qualitative summary of the trend observed in the variance of mechanical strength and fresh properties of concrete with an increase in CB content is described in Fig.  8 , where a positive deviation implies an increase in original value and a negative trend implies a decrease. The figure has not specified the exact deviation values as they vary based on parameters like the type of CB, grade of concrete, and concrete mix used. However, irrespective of these parameters, the trend in deviation has been observed to be similar in all studies.
Fig. 8 Variation in mechanical and fresh properties of concrete with CB [145].

sections.heading: Durability and long-term performance
paragraphs: The durability of CB incorporated concrete is crucial in determining its long-term structural performance, particularly in aggressive environmental conditions. As observed with other concrete properties, a small amount of CB reduces the chlorine penetration depth, indicating an improvement in the concrete microstructure that reduces the permeability, thus restricting the ingress of harmful ions [ 148 ]. However, beyond a certain threshold, excessive CB content leads to aggregation and poor packing, increasing porosity and penetration depth.

This can be attributed to the improvement in the microstructure of the cement matrix due to the slight inclusion of CB, which is discussed in detail in the next section. However, excessive CB content may increase porosity due to agglomeration, thus compromising durability. Beyond chloride ingress, existing studies also suggest that low, well‑dispersed CB dosages can modestly refine the pore structure and slow carbonation and sulfate ingress, whereas high dosages and poor dispersion may accelerate carbonation fronts and local sulfate damage by increasing connectivity of micro‑ and macro‑pores [ 139 ]. Freeze–thaw resistance and scaling behavior likewise depend on how carbon black affects the air-void system, because if carbon black addition alters air entrainment or creates interconnected pores the resistance to freeze–thaw cycles and deicing salts can deteriorate, whereas carefully optimized mixtures can maintain or slightly improve durability performance [ 139 ]. For reinforced systems, the introduction of electrically conductive CB networks raises additional questions regarding corrosion: on the one hand, reduced permeability can slow chloride‑induced corrosion, but on the other, conductive pathways may change macrocell formation and current distribution along steel reinforcement, which remains insufficiently explored [ 149 ]. Further research is required to explore the influence of CB sourced from different production methods and waste streams, ensuring its optimal contribution to mechanical performance and long-term durability.

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis of CB-incorporated concrete
paragraphs: A detailed microstructural analysis is necessary to understand the reason behind CBs’ effect on concrete performance. Techniques including scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) have been employed by several researchers to study the dispersion of CB within the cement matrix [ 39 ,  122 ,  150 ].

The XRD patterns in these studies reveal the presence of three primary hydration products: calcium hydroxide, calcium carbonate, and calcium silicate hydrate (CSH), which are also the dominant phases found in standard concrete. It has been observed that carbon black (CB) does not play a significant role in the hydration process. However, the intensity of these peaks, particularly the CSH peak, tends to increase slightly with the initial addition of CB, suggesting a minor enhancement in the formation of hydration products. Yet, as the CB content increases beyond a certain point, the intensity of these peaks diminishes, indicating a possible inhibitory effect on further hydration. While these findings provide initial insights into the interaction between CB and cement hydration, they remain inconclusive, highlighting the need for further in-depth studies to fully understand the underlying mechanisms. Future research should explore the precise influence of CB on the microstructure and long-term performance of concrete, as well as its potential effects on the durability and mechanical properties of the material.

SEM is commonly used to analyze the micromorphology of concrete and provides visual evidence of the concrete’s amorphous and hexagonal structures. Due to the challenge of distinctly identifying CB particles due to their fine size, EDX techniques are also employed to help determine the concentration of carbon content in the cement matrix [ 122 ]. SEM and EDX techniques’ observations revealed that the interfacial transition zone (ITZ) became more compact, and the pore content decreased as a slight amount of CB was added to the concrete. Through these analyses conducted by several researchers, it has been concluded that CB often acts as nucleation sites for forming cement hydration products. Furthermore, they also validate that the filler effect of CB plays a crucial role in influencing in physical properties of concrete, as discussed in previous sections.

sections.heading: Environmental impact
paragraphs: The environmental impact of incorporating carbon black in concrete presents both challenges and significant sustainability opportunities, particularly when considering the utilization of waste-derived carbon black materials and life cycle assessment perspectives [ 151 ]. Life cycle assessment results demonstrate that using waste carbon black in cement mortar production significantly reduces emissions to the environment, with studies reporting substantial decreases in global warming potential and environmental footprint compared to conventional concrete production [ 152 ]. The recycling of waste carbon black from tire pyrolysis into concrete applications represents a promising environmental strategy, with research indicating that pyrolyzed carbon black derived from waste tires can reduce the negative environmental footprint while providing concrete with enhanced mechanical properties [ 153 ]. Recycled carbon black from scrapped off-the-road tires demonstrates significant potential for developing thermal insulation cement-based mortars, contributing to both waste management solutions and energy-efficient building materials [ 154 ]. The sustainability benefits of carbon black incorporation extend beyond waste utilization, with studies showing that biochar-carbon black hybrid composites can achieve carbon-negative concrete production, potentially reducing over 60 tons of carbon dioxide emissions per ton of concrete [ 155 ]. Environmental life cycle assessment comparisons reveal that concrete incorporating recycled carbon materials shows reduced embodied carbon and improved eco-efficiency compared to conventional concrete systems [ 156 ]. The integration of waste tire constituents including carbon black in geopolymer mortars demonstrates feasible and sustainable alternatives to conventional concrete, with RSM-based environmental assessments confirming reduced environmental impacts [ 157 ]. Research on waste material recycling for self-sensing concretes indicates that incorporating recycled carbon black and other waste materials can contribute to both sustainability goals and circular economy principles in construction applications [ 158 ].

The incorporation of CB in concrete applications has demonstrated significant environmental benefits and potential, particularly in enhancing sustainability [ 159 ]. By repurposing industrial byproducts like CB, landfills are reduced, thereby promoting a circular economy [ 160 ]. Incorporation of CB improvs the mechanical properties of concrete, which reduces the need for repairs and replacements, thereby conserving natural resources and energy. CB’s dual role as a strength enhancer and a conductive material was investigated, noting its application in self-sensing concrete, which allows for real-time monitoring and minimizes waste through preventive maintenance [ 161 ]. The environmental benefits of using CB derived from worn-out tires were highlighted, showcasing its potential to transform hazardous waste into a valuable resource that significantly enhances concrete strength [ 162 ]. Concrete production significantly contributes to global CO 2  emissions, driven primarily by the carbon-intensive process of cement manufacturing. Innovations such as the incorporation of CB into concrete formulations have emerged as viable solutions to reduce this environmental impact. CB enhances the mechanical properties of concrete by improving particle packing and reducing porosity, creating a denser microstructure that increases durability and extends the lifecycle of structures, thus reducing reliance on ordinary Portland cement (OPC) and associated emissions [ 163 ]. Furthermore, CB-modified concretes optimize carbonation where the concrete absorbs atmospheric CO 2  by achieving a balanced microstructure that ensures both durability and effective CO 2  sequestration [ 9 ]. These studies have consistently shown that the GWP decreases as the CB content in concrete increases. Notably, for a 40% replacement of cement with CB, a reduction of up to 35% in GWP has been observed.

On a life-cycle basis, ordinary concrete typically embodies on the order of 200–500 kg CO₂ per m³, with most of these emissions attributable to the cement content. Globally, process emissions from cement production alone reached about 1.5 Gt CO₂ in 2018, corresponding to roughly 4–8% of total anthropogenic CO₂ emissions, which translates to sectoral average intensities of around 0.5–0.8 t CO₂ per ton of cement depending on the scenario and data source [ 164 ]. In parallel, conventional carbon black production is estimated to emit on the order of 2–3 kg of CO₂ (and CO) per kg of product, contributing tens of millions of tons of CO₂ annually at current production volumes [ 165 ]. LCA studies state that partially replace cement with waste or recovered carbon black in mortar or concrete systems show appreciable reductions in cradle-to-grave impacts especially when CB diverts an industrial by-product from landfill and displaces clinker while maintaining acceptable mechanical performance in appropriate, typically lower-strength applications [ 122 ]. In our review, we therefore compare reported mixes on a functional basis (kg CO₂e per m³ of concrete or per MPa·m³), accounting for CB production, transport, service-life carbonation of cementitious matrices, and end-of-life scenarios, to clarify under which conditions CB-modified concretes can deliver net CO₂e savings relative to conventional reference mixes.

However, as discussed in previous sections, increasing the CB content beyond approximately 10% begins to impact on the mechanical properties of concrete negatively. At this optimal replacement level, the reduction in GWP is approximately 9%, which, while beneficial, is not highly significant. These GWP values are based on a cradle-to-gate perspective for concrete production, with the functional unit typically defined as either 1 m³ of concrete or 1 MPa·m³ of load-bearing capacity, and the system boundaries must explicitly include cement production, carbon black (CB) production or recovery, mixing processes, and where relevant the transport and pretreatment of pyrolyzed CB to enable robust comparison with other supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) [ 166 ]. Nonetheless, the long-term environmental benefits of CB incorporation may also extend beyond these initial reductions. In particular, when waste tire‑derived recovered carbon black (rCB) displaces virgin furnace carbon black, LCAs have shown very large relative CO₂ savings at the material level (often > 70% reduction in CB‑related emissions), but these benefits need to be translated carefully to the concrete scale by accounting for pyrolysis energy demand, reactor efficiency, and co‑product allocation [ 167 ]. When compared to traditional SCMs such as fly ash and ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS), CB presents a unique trade-off between mechanical performance and environmental sustainability [ 168 ]. While fly ash and GGBS have proven to be highly effective in reducing GWP (with reductions of up to 51% at high replacement levels), they often come at the cost of decreased compressive strength, as described in Table  4 . However, these SCMs are increasingly constrained by the decarbonization of the power and steel sectors, and several regional assessments have already highlighted emerging shortages and geographic supply risks for high‑quality fly ash, in contrast to the large and persistent global stock of end‑of‑life tires that can serve as feedstock for pyrolytic CB [ 169 ]. Overall, while CB may not match traditional SCMs in terms of environmental impact reduction, its characteristics to improve mechanical performance make it a promising alternative. From a circular‑economy perspective, CB recovered from waste tires can simultaneously divert a problematic waste stream from landfilling or incineration and partially replace both cement and virgin CB, but the net benefit depends on realistic assumptions about mass recovery rates typically 25–40% of tire mass as rCB, quality consistency, and industrial scalability of pyrolysis plants [ 170 ].

Beyond GWP reduction, a limited number of life cycle assessment (LCA) studies have evaluated additional environmental impact parameters, including acidification potential (AP), eutrophication potential (EP), and abiotic depletion potential (ADP). These parameters are predominantly influenced by Portland cement, a major contributor to environmental degradation. AP measures the release of acidic gases during the concrete life cycle, which can lead to soil acidification, water body contamination, and biodiversity harm. EP accounts for excessive nutrient deposition in water bodies, causing ecological imbalance. ADP assesses the environmental burden of natural resource extraction and depletion caused by concrete production. Studies indicate that replacing cement with CB reduces AP, EP, and ADP. For pyrolyzed CB in concrete, these reductions largely arise from lower clinker content and the avoided production of virgin CB, but they must be balanced against the energy and emissions of tire pyrolysis (including fuel use, off‑gas handling, and post‑treatment of rCB), which can partially offset impact reductions if not optimized [ 171 ]. However, similar to the GWP, the decrease is around 7.5% for the optimal amount of CB and is insignificant. However, for around 40% replacement, the reduction in these parameters can reach up to 30%, indicating a more substantial environmental benefit at the cost of mechanical performance [ 37 ]. In addition, pyrolyzed CB can contain concentrated inorganic residues and trace metals from tire formulations, so any large‑scale use in concrete should be accompanied by leaching and ecotoxicity assessments analogous to those conducted for other pyrolyzed wastes, which have shown that metal enrichment during pyrolysis can increase leaching under acidic conditions if not properly immobilized by the cement matrix.

Another key factor influencing the environmental impact of CB-modified concrete is its durability [ 148 ]. As highlighted in  Sect. 4.2.2 , including CB may improve the durability and longevity of concrete structures. This translates into fewer repairs and replacements over the structure’s service life, leading to a further reduction in the environmental impact over time. However, further research is necessary to quantify these long-term effects through emission modeling to understand better the potential environmental benefits associated with CB in concrete. Optimizing the dosage of CBs in concrete is crucial to maximizing its benefits in terms of strength, durability, and environmental performance, paving the way for more sustainable construction practices.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future recommendations
paragraphs: Carbon black (CB), particularly recycled and pyrolytic grades, is increasingly recognized as a multifunctional additive with potential to advance both the performance and sustainability of cementitious materials. At carefully optimized dosages (typically 1–5% by binder mass), CB can refine pore structure, enhance compressive strength, and introduce electrical conductivity for self-sensing applications, all while contributing to circular economy objectives by valorizing waste streams. These benefits, however, are highly dosage- and grade-dependent, and often accompanied by reduced workability and higher water demand. Such challenges can be mitigated through improved dispersion strategies or by combining CB with supplementary cementitious materials such as fly ash. From an environmental standpoint, moderate CB incorporation has been shown to reduce global warming potential (GWP), though excessive substitution risks undermining mechanical performance, underscoring the need for careful balance between environmental gains and structural integrity.

Looking ahead, future research should prioritize scalable dispersion methods and surface functionalization techniques to strengthen CB–C-S-H interactions, as well as systematic mapping of performance windows across CB grades and binder types. Long-term durability studies, coupled with full life cycle assessments under realistic service exposures, remain critical for establishing reliability. Additional opportunities lie in the development of hybrid systems that combine CB with biochar, graphene derivatives, or metallic fibers to unlock synergistic improvements in strength, conductivity, and multifunctionality. Parallel efforts are also needed to standardize self-sensing metrics, tailor rheological behavior for emerging applications such as 3D concrete printing, and link CB’s nanostructure to macro-scale performance through multiscale modeling and advanced characterization. All or some of these directions will help bridge the gap between laboratory findings and practical adoption, paving the way for CB-enabled, low-carbon, and intelligent infrastructure solutions.
